title: The Scale Panic

scenario.situation: Traffic is growing and the team fears the PostgreSQL database won't keep up. The lead wants to migrate the core catalog and orders to Cassandra "for web-scale".
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead believes relational Postgres is a scaling dead-end and that NoSQL is required to handle growth.
scenario.question: Does the workload actually exceed what Postgres can do, or is the migration solving an imaginary limit?

decisions.prompt: How do you approach the datastore decision?

options.label: Begin migrating catalog and orders to Cassandra
options.detail: Start denormalizing the schema for a NoSQL model.
options.consequence: You start denormalizing a richly relational schema before measuring whether Postgres is anywhere near its limits — trading joins and transactions away to solve a bottleneck you haven't confirmed exists.
options.divergenceCost: Began a NoSQL migration before measuring whether the relational database was the bottleneck.

options.label: Measure the real workload — data size, query patterns, current headroom
options.detail: Quantify volume, access pattern, and how hard the current DB is actually working.
options.consequence: You measure: ~60 GB of data, ~2,000 queries/sec at peak, and a workload full of multi-table joins and transactional order writes. Postgres runs at 30% CPU with plenty of headroom, and the access pattern is deeply relational.

options.label: Read Cassandra case studies from large-scale companies
options.detail: Study how hyperscalers run NoSQL at massive volume.
options.consequence: You find impressive stories from companies operating at 1000x your data and traffic — inspiring, and completely irrelevant to a 60 GB, 2k-qps workload.
options.divergenceCost: Borrowed scaling decisions from companies whose workload is nothing like yours.

options.label: Add a caching layer in front of Postgres now
options.detail: Introduce a cache to relieve pressure preemptively.
options.consequence: A cache might help later, but bolting one on before you've found any bottleneck adds a moving part and a consistency headache to solve a problem you haven't demonstrated.
options.divergenceCost: Added infrastructure to relieve pressure you hadn't shown the database was under.

decisions.prompt: You've measured the workload. Which reading decides whether Postgres is truly at its limit?

artifact.title: Peak queries per second (headline trend)
artifact.caption: QPS has nearly doubled year over year — the growth curve that sparked the panic. But a rising trend says nothing about whether you're near the ceiling.

options.label: The growth rate of traffic
options.detail: Project the trend forward and act on how fast it's climbing.
options.consequence: Traffic is clearly climbing, which feels alarming — but a growth rate with no reference to capacity is a scary-looking line with no ceiling marked. You could be at 5% of the limit or 95%; the trend alone can't tell you.
options.divergenceCost: Reacted to a growth trend without measuring it against the database's actual capacity.

options.label: Current load as a fraction of demonstrated capacity, given the access pattern
options.detail: Benchmark how much of this query mix Postgres sustains, and where you sit on it.
options.consequence: Benchmarked on the same hardware, Postgres sustains ~15,000 qps of this query mix before latency degrades; you're at 2,000. You're using ~13% of proven capacity, with vertical scaling and read-replicas untouched — and the join/transaction-heavy pattern is exactly what Cassandra is worst at.

artifact.title: Current load vs proven Postgres capacity (thousands of qps)
artifact.caption: Current load is ~13% of demonstrated capacity on the existing setup, before read-replicas or a larger instance. The relational database has years of headroom for this workload.

options.label: Approve the Cassandra migration to get ahead of scale
options.detail: Move to NoSQL now so scale never becomes a fire.
options.consequence: You trade away joins, foreign keys, and transactional integrity — everything the order system depends on — to escape a limit you're at 13% of. The app gets harder to build and correctness bugs creep in, all to solve a non-problem.
options.divergenceCost: Traded relational guarantees the app needs to escape a limit that's years away.

options.label: Stay on Postgres, name the scaling path and the real trigger to reconsider
options.detail: Lay out replicas then partitioning, and define when NoSQL would actually be warranted.
options.consequence: You advise staying relational, lay out the incremental scaling path — read replicas, then vertical scale, then partitioning — and set a concrete trigger (sustained load approaching a set fraction of capacity, or a genuinely non-relational workload) for revisiting NoSQL. The team keeps its guarantees and its roadmap.

insight: The migration was a solution in search of a problem: at 60 GB and 2,000 qps the database sat at ~13% of demonstrated capacity, with replicas and vertical scaling untouched — and the join- and transaction-heavy access pattern is precisely what Cassandra sacrifices. A rising traffic curve triggered the panic, but a growth rate means nothing without the capacity ceiling to measure it against. The lesson is to pick a datastore from the access pattern and the load relative to proven capacity, not from a fear of scale or the gravity of 'web-scale' NoSQL — and to keep relational guarantees until a workload actually outgrows them.
